name: us-state-tax
description: Dependency-free US state AND LOCAL individual income tax engine for tax years 2025 and 2026, covering 27 states and 1,033 local income taxes: New York City, Yonkers, all 24 Maryland jurisdictions, all 92 Indiana counties, all 24 Michigan cities, all 679 Ohio municipalities and all 214 Ohio school districts - more taxing jurisdictions than the rest of the United States put together. Ohio taxes one paycheck on THREE different bases and they disagree about what a wage is: the state taxes federal AGI as adjusted, a municipality taxes qualifying wages (box 5 of the W-2, gross of a 401(k) deferral), and a school district taxes either modified AGI less exemptions - which adds the business income deduction back, so it reaches income the state return does not - or wages as included in modified AGI, which is box 1, net of that same deferral. Models what rate tables leave out: Ohio, whose printed schedule is DISCONTINUOUS - a filer with $26,050 of taxable nonbusiness income owes nothing and one with $26,050.01 owes $342.00, because O.R.C. 5747.02(A)(3) charges the constant whole on the first dollar of the band, so reading the three rows as marginal brackets understates every Ohio filer by $342 - and which steps a SECOND time by $18.69 at $100,000 because HB 96 re-based the lower constant from $360.69 to $342.00 and left the upper one at what $360.69 chained to; where the first $250,000 of business income is deducted and the excess taxed at a flat 3%, so $250,000 of Schedule C profit costs $0 and $250,000 of wages costs $7,022.45; where the exemption chart and every credit limit are read against a modified AGI that adds the business deduction straight back; where the $20 exemption credit is claimable ONLY by a childless single filer in a $1,550 window of income and the joint filing credit's 20% row is unreachable arithmetic; and where 679 municipalities charge 0.45% to 3.00% on QUALIFYING WAGES - box 5 of the W-2, which a 401(k) deferral does not reduce, costing a Columbus saver $612.50 a year that box 1 never shows - so the municipal tax is the LARGER half of every Ohio return below $126,408.32 of income, an Ohio retiree owes their municipality nothing, and a commuter pays the higher of the two rates whichever way they commute because Ohio has no statutory resident credit and no half rate for nonresidents; Michigan, where Detroit charges residents 2.4% on a base the MI-1040 does not contain, where the personal exemption has been the $600 the Legislature set in 1964 and is worth $14.40 against an indexed $5,800 state exemption, and where a Lansing resident commuting to Detroit pays 70% more city tax than one working at home; Indiana, where the average county rate is 1.914% against a state rate of 3.00%; Maryland, where every resident owes a county income tax of 2.25%-3.30%, where Frederick County's bracket selects one rate that applies to the WHOLE income so one dollar at $150,000 costs $360.03, and where the new 2% capital gains surtax is a test rather than a floor so one dollar of AGI at $350,000 can cost $6,933.08; Massachusetts, which every rate table reports as a flat 5% and which taxes short-term capital gains at 8.5%; New Jersey, whose retirement exclusion ends in a wall that costs a joint retiree $1,381 on one dollar; CalEITC, which is a triangle with no plateau; New York City's 3.078%-3.876% resident tax and its 30%-to-10% sliding earned income credit; the Yonkers surcharge of 16.75% of the state tax; which federal figure each state starts from; which federal deductions it adds back; and the credit phase-outs that make Utah's and Pennsylvania's flat taxes anything but flat. Every figure cited to the statute or state release it came from, and every carried-forward figure flagged as provisional.
